The cylindrical specimen used in the experiments was 16 cm long and made of commercial aluminum.
The actual length of the specimen considered in the calculations was 15.7 cm, which is the distance between the lower thermocouple and the upper base.
The thermal guard used was a hollow cylinder made of the same material as the specimen, with an outer diameter of 4 cm and an inner diameter of 2 cm.
The temperature was measured at two different positions in the specimen: one thermocouple was placed 2 mm from the lower base, and the other was placed at the upper base.
The heat source was applied at the lower base of the specimen, either using an electric resistive coil or a lighter.
The temperature data was recorded at 10-second intervals during the heating of the specimen, which lasted approximately 3 minutes.
The numerical method used a recurrence relation to solve the thermal transport equation in the cylindrical specimen, with the temperature measured by the lower thermocouple as the boundary condition.
The thermal diffusivity value that provided the best agreement between the calculated and experimentally measured temperatures at the upper base was 0.79 cm^2/s.
Repeated measurements on the same specimen yielded a thermal diffusivity value of (0.75 ± 0.07) cm^2/s, which is in good agreement with values obtained in more controlled environments.
The numerical recurrence relation used in the calculations is relatively simple and can be implemented by undergraduate students on a personal computer.
The experimental setup has a low cost, allowing for the preparation of multiple replicas without excessive financial burden on the laboratory.
The method is suitable for materials with high thermal conductivity, such as aluminum, but may not be as suitable for low-conducting materials.
The paper mentions the possibility of convective heat flows during the heating of the specimen, which can introduce some dispersion in the measured values.
The theoretical model assumes a one-dimensional heat transfer, which may not fully capture the actual heat transfer in the cylindrical specimen.
The paper suggests that the experimental setup could be improved by creating a small box around it and evacuating it to reduce the effects of convective heat flows.
